title: Compassion

segments.voice: Yesterday, a God who suffers: Jesus weeping near the tomb of his friend. Your line was god in the pain. Who did you picture, not alone? Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

A funeral is coming out through the gate of a town called Nain. A young man is being carried out on a bier. Luke gives the detail that makes it unbearable: he was "the only son of his mother, and she was a widow." A crowd from the town walks with her. Coming up the road the other way is Jesus, with his own crowd behind him. Two processions meet at the gate. Nobody asks him for anything. Luke says that when he saw her, something moved in him before he said a word or lifted a hand. Today: compassion.
screen: `A FUNERAL AT THE GATE OF NAIN.`

segments.voice: First, the English word. Some readers hear two Latin pieces inside compassion: with, and suffering. Suffer with. Not pity handed down from above. Feeling it from beside. Next, the Gospels' word goes lower still. In the King James Bible: "And when the Lord saw her, he had compassion on her, and said unto her, Weep not." The Greek verb behind had compassion is splanchnizomai, and some readers hear in it the inward parts, the gut: being moved in your insides. Luke says the same of the Samaritan who stops for the man left half dead on the Jericho road: "he had compassion on him." And of the father in the parable of the lost son: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Then notice the order. Every time, the feeling comes first, and then the body moves. Jesus touches the bier, and the young man sits up. The Samaritan goes to him and binds up his wounds. The father runs. Compassion in these stories isn't a mood. It ends in the hands and feet. Last, Paul turns it into a job for ordinary people. To the Romans: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep." To the Galatians: "Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ." With. One another. Staying close. Some Christians link it to yesterday: if God suffers with people, then following him means doing the same. It doesn't answer why there is suffering. It answers a different question: what now? Suffer with.

Here's the practice: stay with someone suffering. Settle, and breathe. Choose someone who is hurting and whom you could actually reach: by a call, a visit, a message. It may be the person you showed up for after Job's day; this time the practice is about staying, not arriving. Picture the conversation. Notice the pull to keep it short, to cheer them up, to change the subject, to fix it. Now picture yourself staying instead. Listening longer than is comfortable. Letting a silence sit. Weeping with them, if it comes to that. If you pray, you can bring them to God, in your own words or your church's. If you don't, let the picture of staying be enough for now. The bell holds the time.
Compassion. Suffering with someone: being moved inside, and then staying close.
Your line: suffer with. Today, reach the person you thought of, and stay a little longer than is easy. Day one thousand three hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: Christians practice compassion by visiting the sick and grieving, bringing meals, sitting with the dying and giving to those in need; churches organize care teams, hospital chaplaincies and works of mercy.

original.note: Greek: to be moved with compassion, a word some readers link with the inward parts. used of Jesus at Nain, the Samaritan, and the father of the lost son.

trapdoor: what you thought: compassion means feeling sorry for someone.
what it means: suffering with them: being moved inside, then staying close.
what a scholar hears: splanchnizomai, a word some readers tie to the gut, used for Jesus at Nain, the Samaritan on the Jericho road, and the father running to his son.

notes: The Latin 'with + suffering' reading of 'compassion' is attributed to 'some readers', under the claims rule; the index hook states it as the meaning. Confirm.
splanchnizomai and its link to splanchna (inward parts) attributed to 'lexicons'; confirm. Confirm Luke uses the same verb at 7:13, 10:33 and 15:20.
Hook: 'Nobody asks him for anything' reflects Luke 7:11–13, where no request is recorded; confirm.
The Samaritan is named without the priest and Levite, to avoid using them as a foil.

Editor pass: the splanchnizomai etymology is now attributed to 'some readers' rather than 'lexicons' (claims rule), and the claim that Luke uses the same Greek verb is replaced by the KJV text of Luke 10:33 (now quoted and cited); cut 'small' (not in Luke 7); 'Christians link it' became 'some Christians'; the practice now builds on day 1378 instead of repeating it.

Audit (fresh reviewer): 'the Samaritan kneels' is not in Luke 10:34 ('went to him, and bound up his wounds'); now follows the text. The com + pati etymology is standard and could be stated plainly rather than as 'some readers hear'.
